title: Patti Schutte says AI is giving sales teams more data and worse results
excerpt: Patti Schutte says sales teams have more AI-generated talking points than ever, yet deals stall when reps never internalize the deal.
content_html:
Most people know the difference between reciting a fact and truly understanding it. In sales organizations today, that gap is costing companies their most promising deals.

Patti Schutte has spent the past year listening to recorded sales calls across the enterprise teams she coaches. She keeps hearing the same problem. Salespeople have more research, more data and more AI-generated talking points than any generation before them. Yet the deals are stalling anyway.

“AI gives you information based on past data, and you are selling for future state,” says Schutte, founder of Be Brilliant Presentation Group and creator of the Resultations Method®.

One of Schutte’s clients recently noticed their discovery calls had tripled. Their closed deals had not moved at all.

When she reviewed the call recordings, the pattern was unmistakable. The account managers on the calls sounded like actors reciting a script rather than people in conversation. They were delivering accurate but strangely lifeless AI-generated talking points.

“Just like somebody who memorized their movie script lines, they didn’t deliver the lines,” Schutte says. “Instead, you’re tuning out because they’re dictating their lines without connection.”

The problem was not that the account managers lacked information. It was that many of them had never internalized it.

“Internalize means that I know information so well I can hug it. I can feel it,” Schutte says. “It’s no longer abstract, and I’m no longer having to go, ’Oh, let me look that up.’”

Internalization, in Schutte’s definition, means knowing a deal and the person on the other end well enough that a salesperson no longer has to look anything up. It also means they can stay fluid when a conversation takes a turn.

Knowing the deal

She offers an example. A prospect brushes off a costly problem, saying the company hired a full-time employee to deal with it. An account manager who has internalized the deal catches that moment immediately, calls it out and immediately dives deeper.

“You just told me you had to hire a full-time, 40-hour-a-week employee to solve this problem? That means it’s costing you hundreds and thousands of dollars on a regular basis,” Schutte says. “And so let’s dive into that a little bit more.”

Schutte calls these moments golden nuggets, the comments prospects drop that point to a real problem. In one recorded call, a prospect who took the meeting for free AirPods mentioned the company was shrinking.

“It was the only nugget they gave that could potentially open up to anything else,” Schutte says.

She is helping one client turn a rigid script into a narrative with branches. It is built around a hypothesis about the big shift inside the prospect’s organization.

“AI can help you with that, but you still need to internalize it and you still need to know this deal well enough and the prospect well enough to be fluid,” Schutte says.

The confidence to pivot

Knowing when to pivot requires something many sales teams are overlooking: the confidence to trust their own judgment.

Schutte sees this in coaching sessions. Salespeople with all the information they need still hesitate to ask questions, challenge assumptions or explore an unexpected answer.

“One rep told me a question I was suggesting they ask in the future felt too aggressive. It wasn’t too aggressive; they just didn’t feel confident asking it without something or someone telling them it was okay first,” Schutte says. “That willingness to ask more questions, dive deeper, challenge the norm and go for it, I’m not seeing as much as I used to.”

The danger, in Schutte’s view, lies not in AI itself but in account managers who rely so heavily on having the right information and the right words that they lose the ability to steer a conversation without them.

“The best salespeople I’ve worked with all do the same thing,” Schutte says. “They paint the picture between where a company is now and what life looks like after the solution is in place. AI can paint a picture of the future. Great salespeople make the buyer see themselves in it.”

Where deals are won

That future state is where deals are won or lost. Schutte frequently sees enterprise deals stall not because a competitor offers a better solution but because the buyer never develops enough clarity or confidence to decide. Great salespeople help buyers understand what the problem is costing them, what happens if nothing changes and what is possible on the other side of a decision.

To build that judgment, Schutte often asks clients to write a quick note after each call on what happened, what worked, what they missed and what they would do differently. The exercise pushes account managers to develop their own judgment instead of relying on AI-generated summaries.

One CEO who sits in on sales calls told Schutte that listening alone is enough to tell which salespeople are implementing her coaching. Those who do are regularly seeing better results, often becoming the top producers of the month or quarter.

Schutte is not arguing for less AI. She believes it can make salespeople more prepared, more informed and more efficient. But preparation is not the same as performance, and information is not the same as influence.

The companies that benefit most from AI will not necessarily be the ones giving their sales teams the most information. They will be the ones developing people who know what to do with it.

AI can prepare a salesperson for a conversation. It is still the human who must turn that conversation into a decision.

Patti Schutte is the founder of Be Brilliant Presentation Group and creator of the Resultations Method®, a framework that helps professionals turn high-stakes presentation moments into measurable business results. To learn more, visit bebrilliantpresentationgroup.com or connect with her on LinkedIn at linkedin.com/in/pattischutte.
